title: Produce safety technician hosts workshop amid cyclospora outbreak - NewsBreak
text:
By Zack Priehs Shajaka Shelton ,
1 hours ago MERIDIAN TOWNSHIP, Mich. (WLNS) — As Michigan has confirmed more than 3,700 cases of cyclosporiasis statewide , food safety experts have some recommendations for how to minimize your risk of infection.
Health officials work to pinpoint where it started and how it spread. Meanwhile, produce safety technician Morgan Anderson hosted a food safety workshop Wednesday. She serves as a free resource to farmers who have questions about produce safety.
Produce at the farmer’s market (WLNS) The workshop, hosted at the Meridian Township Farmer’s Market, served to educate the public on best practices when it comes to cleaning produce.
“So produce washing we’ll be touching on a lot today, as well as hand washing and cleaning and sanitizing of your prep space,” Anderson told workshop attendees.
While the workshop was scheduled before the current outbreak began, much of the information is still relevant.
“Basic hand washing and then, of course, cleaning and washing of the produce itself,” Anderson said. “But also of your food contact surfaces in the kitchen or wherever it is that you’re preparing food. How you are washing your silverware, your knives, your cutting board especially.”
Experts at Michigan State University, like Wade Syers, a food safety specialist at Michigan State University, also shared some guidance with 6 News.
A sign for Tuesday’s food safety event. (WLNS) “I really am just being diligent about following the established food safety practices for produce,” Syers said “I am washing my hands before preparing any fruits or vegetables.”
Syers added that he’s rinsing all produce under running water, and if possible, scrubbing it with a produce brush. He adds that the parasite often spreads through raw produce so cooking your food can help a lot as well.
Anderson said even though Wednesday’s workshop wasn’t about cyclosporiasis, specicfically, there’s no better time than now to make sure your food is safe.
The cyclosporiasis parasite. (Centers for Disease Control) “It’s really relevant to say, ‘Hey let’s be mindful of how are we preparing our food at home. Are we washing our hands? Where are we getting our food?'” Adnerson said.
Syers tells 6 News he’s been keeping different types of produce separate from each other as an extra precaution.
Rebecca Schein, a pediatric infectious disease physician with MSU Health Care recommends washing with plenty of water.
“Use large amounts of water. Dilution is the solution to pollution.” said Schein. “There is no evidence to support cleaning with vinegar or anything else.”
